title: Putting up a Christmas tree this weekend? A four-inch trunk needs a gallon-size stand
excerpt: Mississippi’s tree guide gives a simple sizing rule. A fresh tree can drink enough in its first days to need more than one refill a day.
locality: Consumer service for households in Pontotoc County, Mississippi, where Carnes Farms sells Christmas trees.

facts.statement: For families bringing a Christmas tree home from Carnes Farms in Pontotoc or another grower this weekend, the first measurement to take is across the cut end of the trunk. Christmas is four weeks from Friday, and that measurement helps determine how much water the stand should hold. Mississippi’s Genuine MS tree guide calls for a quart of water capacity for each inch of diameter. A four-inch trunk needs a stand that holds at least a gallon.
facts.evidence: Genuine MS identifies Carnes Farms as a Pontotoc Christmas tree grower. State agriculture guide and university article both specify one quart per inch of diameter. Four quarts equal one gallon. November 27 to December 25 is 28 days.
facts.statistics: 4 weeks, 1 quart per inch, 1 gallon for a 4-inch trunk.

paragraphs.text: For families bringing a Christmas tree home from Carnes Farms in Pontotoc or another grower this weekend, the first measurement to take is across the cut end of the trunk. Christmas is four weeks from Friday, and that measurement helps determine how much water the stand should hold. Mississippi’s Genuine MS tree guide calls for a quart of water capacity for each inch of diameter. A four-inch trunk needs a stand that holds at least a gallon.

Give the trunk a fresh, straight cut and put it in water right away. If the tree comes home before the stand is ready, the state agriculture guide recommends keeping it in a bucket of water in the meantime. Use plain tap water in the stand. Mississippi State says drilling holes in the base does nothing to help the tree take up water.

The height of the water matters as much as the size of the stand. Keep the cut end submerged and check it several times a day, especially just after bringing the tree home. Mississippi State Extension says a tree can take up as much as two gallons in a day during those first few days. A gallon-size stand may need more than one fill.

Before stringing the lights, leave at least three feet between the tree and fireplaces, radiators, heat vents or space heaters. Keep a clear path to the door. Mississippi State Extension recommends checking used light strings for damaged wires and unplugging them before bed or before leaving home. The U.S. Fire Administration advises taking a dry tree out of the house.

image.alt_text: At a quart per inch of trunk diameter, a three-inch trunk needs three quarts of water capacity, a four-inch trunk needs a gallon and a six-inch trunk needs a gallon and a half.
